identity.title: Jugular venous pressure elevated (>8 cm H2O / >3 cm above sternal angle); low/flat JVP as the negative

technique.how: Recline the patient at 30-45 degrees (adjust until the top of the pulsation is visible), turn the head slightly left, and use tangential light to find the top of the internal jugular column. Measure its vertical height above the sternal angle; >3 cm above the angle (about >8 cm H2O total) is elevated.
technique.prerequisites: Adequate light, exposed neck, patient relaxed and breathing quietly; identify the venous (biphasic, non-palpable, falls with inspiration, occludable) rather than carotid pulsation.
technique.contraindications: None; avoid firm neck pressure in patients with carotid disease.

interpretation.positive_finding: A venous column >3 cm above the sternal angle indicates raised right atrial pressure and, in chronic heart failure, usually raised left-sided filling pressure (PCWP >=18 mmHg). It substantially raises the probability of heart failure as the cause of acute dyspnea.
interpretation.negative_finding: A flat or normal JVP lowers but does not exclude heart failure; sensitivity is modest (roughly 0.2-0.7 across ED studies) and pooled sensitivity in ED series stays below 0.55.
interpretation.pitfalls: Confusing carotid with venous pulsation, misjudging the sternal angle-to-atrium distance (varies with position), and failing to see a very high column (look for earlobe pulsation) or a very low one (lie the patient flatter). Isolated RV failure, tricuspid disease, tamponade or constriction raise JVP without left-sided congestion.
interpretation.changes_what: Elevated JVP moves dyspnea/edema toward acute HF or RV/pericardial disease and away from hypovolemia; a flat JVP in hypotension favors hypovolemia/sepsis over cardiogenic causes.

sources.citation: Butman SM, Ewy GA, Standen JR, Kern KB, Hahn E. Bedside cardiovascular examination in patients with severe chronic heart failure: importance of rest or inducible jugular venous distension. J Am Coll Cardiol 1993;22(4):968-74.
Signs and symptoms in adult patients with acute dyspnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Emerg Med 2018;25(1):3-11 (author list not retrievable via abstract tool; confirmed by PMID/DOI).

Mant J, Doust J, Roalfe A, et al. Systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis of diagnosis of heart failure, with modelling of implications of different diagnostic strategies in primary care. Health Technol Assess 2009;13(32):1-207.
Wang CS, FitzGerald JM, Schulzer M, Mak E, Ayas NT. Does this dyspneic patient in the emergency department have congestive heart failure? JAMA 2005;294(15):1944-56.
Cook DJ, Simel DL. The Rational Clinical Examination. Does this patient have abnormal central venous pressure? JAMA 1996;275(8):630-4.
Mueller C, Frana B, Scholer A, Laule-Kilian K, Perruchoud AP. Emergency diagnosis of congestive heart failure: impact of signs and symptoms. Can J Cardiol 2005;21(11):921-4.

estimates.target_condition: Elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (>=18 mmHg)
estimates.population: 52 patients with severe chronic heart failure undergoing in-hospital transplant evaluation; index finding = jugular venous distension at rest OR inducible by the abdominojugular test
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.81/(1-0.80) = 4.05; LR- = (1-0.81)/0.80 = 0.24 from reported sensitivity 81% and specificity 80% (CIs not reported in abstract)
estimates.quote: had the best combination of sensitivity (81%), specificity (80%) and predictive accuracy (81%) for elevation of the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure

estimates.target_condition: Heart failure as cause of acute dyspnea
estimates.population: Adults with a new episode of acute dyspnea; 8 ED studies, 4737 patients; HF prevalence 25-59%
estimates.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of HF per included studies (varied)
estimates.quote: Elevated jugular venous pressure (0.88, pooled odds ratio: 7), added third heart sound (0.97), and lung crepitations (0.77, pooled odds ratio: 11)

estimates.target_condition: Heart failure (new diagnosis) in primary care
estimates.population: Patients with suspected heart failure in primary care; individual patient data meta-analysis of 9 studies
estimates.reference_standard: Echocardiography / expert panel per included studies
estimates.quote: orthopnoea (89%), oedema (72%), elevated jugular venous pressure (70%), cardiomegaly (85%), added heart sounds (99%), lung crepitations (81%)

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal JVP to withhold treatment for suspected heart failure, or declare a shocked patient hypovolemic when the neck cannot be adequately examined (obesity, short neck, column above the jaw).
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Elevated JVP with hypotension, clear lungs and tachycardia suggests tamponade, RV infarction or massive PE and needs immediate echo/POCUS rather than diuresis.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Agreement between examiners is only fair-to-moderate; clinicians systematically underestimate high venous pressures (Cook & Simel RCE).

extraction_notes: Wang 2005 (RCE) reports JVD LR+ ~5.1 in its evidence table, but JAMA full text is not accessible through this tool, so the table value is not entered; only abstract-visible numbers were used. Cook & Simel 1996 has no abstract on PubMed; cited for technique/interobserver context only. Butman 1993 index finding combines JVD at rest with AJR-inducible JVD, so it is labeled as such rather than as resting JVD alone; LRs computed from rounded sens/spec. The Eur J Emerg Med 2018 review gives only a sensitivity range (0.19-0.70), so sensitivity is left null. Mant 2009 gives specificity 70% without a JVP-specific sensitivity. Mueller 2005 (Can J Cardiol, ED n=452) reports OR 4.3 for elevated JVP, not an LR, so it is cited without an estimate.
